lines: A team keeps a spreadsheet of which table feeds which, updated by hand whenever someone remembers to.
Nobody on that team fully trusts it, because nobody can prove it's actually still accurate.
A different system answers the exact same question a totally different way: by asking the data itself what it depends on.
That one distinction is this whole topic.
Here's the same real pipeline, written two different ways, counted for real rather than just described.
One version wires three stages together as a graph of the data products themselves.
The other wires those same three stages together as a sequence of actions to run, one after another.
Counting only the lines that actually connect one stage's output to the next stage's input: three lines for the first version, four for the second.
Before the next reveal, here's something worth guessing at.
A planted bad row sits in the data -- a number that should never go negative, flipped negative on purpose.
A quality check attached to the pipeline is built specifically to catch exactly that kind of bad row.
When that check catches it and fails, does the rest of the pipeline stop running?
steps.answer: No. The pipeline still runs to completion. The check reports a failure -- it doesn't act as a gate the rest of the run has to pass through first.

lines: Watch that exact scenario run for real, against a live install, not simulated.
The bad row is planted, the pipeline runs end to end, and it succeeds overall.
At the same time, the quality check attached to the middle stage reports failure, and names exactly one bad row caught.
Fix that one row and run the identical pipeline again: the same check now reports success.
steps.takeaway: A failing check doesn't stop a pipeline. It's a report attached to the data, not a gate in front of it.

lines: One more thing worth guessing before it's shown.
The last stage of this pipeline depends on the middle stage, which depends on the first stage.
Nothing here built or updated any separate diagram tracking which stage feeds which.
Can the system still correctly answer what feeds the last stage, all the way back to the start?
steps.answer: Yes, directly. The dependencies were already declared once, on the data itself, so asking for that chain of dependencies is just asking the same structure that already exists.

lines: Ask it directly, for real, right now.
What does the pipeline's final stage depend on, all the way back?
The answer comes back immediately: the middle stage, and the first stage before that.
No separate lineage tool was built, run, or kept in sync to produce that answer.
steps.takeaway: Lineage isn't a separate system here. It's the same dependency graph the pipeline already declared.

lines: Worth naming two more things before moving on.
This system's own packaging and scaffolding layer, for assembling new projects quickly, reached full general release status in a recent version, after a period as a release candidate.
But not every job fits this data-product shape. Sending an email, or calling an outside payment system, doesn't produce a table or a file anyone would call a data product.
Purely operational work -- a deployment step, a cleanup job -- doesn't fit that shape either, and is usually handled outside it instead.
Pulling the whole comparison together now.
One way of building a pipeline wires together the actions that need to run, one after another.
The other way wires together the data products themselves, and lets the actions follow from that.
Choosing the second way is what makes a lineage graph fall out automatically -- at the cost of a model that doesn't fit every single kind of work.
steps.takeaway: The asset graph isn't a prettier task graph. It's a different answer to what the nodes even are.

lines: Back to the exact pipeline this all started with.
A fourth stage joins it now, declaring its own dependency on the final stage from before.
Everything shown so far only ever had three stages declaring their own upstream.
Does adding this fourth stage require building or updating anything to correctly derive its lineage?
steps.answer: No. The mechanism doesn't depend on how many stages already exist. The new stage declares its own single dependency, and the same graph-derivation that worked for three stages keeps working automatically for four.
